title: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT MENSTRUATION WITHOUT PRETENDING WOMEN’S BODIES DON’T EXIST
paragraphs: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT MENSTRUATION WITHOUT PRETENDING WOMEN’S BODIES DON’T EXIST
And when Jesus met a bleeding woman, He did something shame could never do: He called her “Daughter.”
There are subjects Christians can discuss from a pulpit without anyone shifting uncomfortably in their seat.
Blood—as long as it is the blood of a lamb, the blood of a sacrifice, or the blood of Jesus.
But say the word menstruation and suddenly an ordinary function of the female body becomes something people whisper about.
Something young girls sometimes learn to feel embarrassed about before they are old enough to understand why.
And yet there is something almost startling waiting in the pages of Scripture.
The Bible does not pretend women do not bleed.
Without acting as though God somehow becomes embarrassed by the bodies He created.

And if you have ever been made to feel ashamed simply because your body functions like a woman's body, you need to stay with me—because eventually we are going to meet a woman whose bleeding lasted not several days...
And what Jesus did when she touched Him tells us something breathtaking about the heart of God.
But before we get to Jesus, we have to walk through Leviticus.
Because tucked inside the laws that many Christians rush past is a sentence remarkably direct about menstruation.
וְאִשָּׁה כִּי־תִהְיֶה זָבָה דָּם יִהְיֶה זֹבָהּ בִּבְשָׂרָהּ
Ve'ishah ki tihyeh zavah, dam yihyeh zovah biv'sarah...
In straightforward terms: when a woman has a discharge and that discharge from her body is blood, Scripture gives instructions concerning her menstrual state.
The passage uses the Hebrew נִדָּה — niddah.

Translation requires care here. The word has been understood in relation to separation, menstrual status, or ritual impurity, and scholars have debated its precise nuance. What we should not do is casually turn the word into a declaration that the woman herself is morally filthy. Leviticus is dealing with categories of ritual purity and impurity within Israel's covenant worship, not declaring menstruation a personal sin.
Because somewhere along the way, people can take a biblical category and attach an unbiblical emotion to it.
God said something was ritually unclean.
Those are not the same statement.
And the context makes that impossible to ignore.
Read the chapter instead of isolating the woman.
Leviticus 15 also discusses male bodily discharges. The chapter begins with instructions concerning a man experiencing a discharge from his body.
This is not Scripture pointing at women and saying, “Women are dirty.”
This is Scripture taking embodied human existence seriously.
God was not embarrassed to legislate around realities that religious people sometimes become embarrassed even to mention.
The God who designed ovaries knew ovaries existed.
The God who formed the uterus was not surprised by the menstrual cycle.
The God who created blood was not horrified when He saw blood.
Female biology was never hidden information from its Creator.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that sentence more than they expected.
Because maybe your first period did not feel sacred.
Maybe you stained your clothes at school.
Maybe you learned to wrap sanitary products in layers of paper so nobody would know what you were carrying.
Maybe you were taught that periods were “dirty” without anybody explaining what Scripture actually meant when it discussed ritual impurity.
Maybe you have cried in a bathroom because your period arrived again when you desperately wanted to become pregnant.
Or maybe you cried because it did not arrive.
Maybe menopause has changed your body in ways nobody prepared you for.
Maybe miscarriage introduced you to a kind of blood you never wanted to see.
And maybe some of the deepest moments of your life have happened behind a locked bathroom door where nobody else knew you were crying.
And Scripture is far more comfortable acknowledging embodied human existence than many religious cultures have been.
Mark tells us about a woman whose condition was far beyond an ordinary menstrual cycle.
γυνὴ οὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος δώδεκα ἔτη
Gynē ousa en rhysei haimatos dōdeka etē.
A woman who had been suffering from a flow of blood for twelve years.
Stop reading for a moment and imagine living inside those words.
Mark tells us she had suffered greatly under many physicians and spent what she had, yet instead of improving she had grown worse.
The constant awareness of your own body.
The hope every morning that perhaps today it had stopped.
And the crushing discovery that it hadn't.
This woman was not an interesting theological illustration.
There are people reading this who understand that kind of tired.
Maybe your bleeding is not physical.
You have been hemorrhaging emotionally for years.
People see you smiling at church.
They do not see what happens in the car afterward.
They do not know the marriage is bleeding.
They do not know your faith has been bleeding.
They do not know your soul is exhausted.
People hear you say, “God is good.”
They do not hear the question you whisper at 2:13 in the morning:
Twelve years can happen inside a person without appearing on a calendar.
Some wounds bleed where nobody can see them.
And that is why what happens next is so powerful.
There is a crowd pressing around Him, yet Jesus asks who touched Him.
The disciples essentially point out the obvious: everyone is touching You.
But Jesus knows this touch was different.
Mark says she approaches in fear and trembling.
And here is the moment I cannot get away from.
Jesus could have simply healed her and continued walking.
He could have made the miracle private.
He could have let her disappear anonymously into the crowd.
He turns toward the woman whose body had made her life a nightmare...
The Greek of Mark 5:34 begins His response with one astonishing word:
The verb σῴζω — sōzō, represented here by σέσωκέν, can carry the sense of saving, delivering, or making well. Jesus then tells her to go in peace and be whole from her affliction.
But don't rush past the first word.
Before He speaks about the healing...
The woman who had been defined by bleeding is addressed according to belonging.
Not the embarrassing woman in the crowd.
Can you imagine what that word sounded like after twelve years?
Maybe she had forgotten what tenderness sounded like.
And this is where the Gospel becomes bigger than a conversation about menstruation.
Because every one of us has something we desperately want to hide.
Maybe an abortion you have never told anyone about.
Maybe sexual abuse you survived and somehow learned to blame yourself for.
Maybe you know exactly how to lift your hands during worship while hiding a life that is quietly falling apart.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
We even hide from the God who already knows where we are.
But the Gospel is not God standing at a distance shouting, “Clean yourself before you come closer.”
The Gospel is that while humanity could not rescue itself, God came near in Jesus Christ.
Menstruation is not a sin requiring repentance.
Your female body does not need forgiveness for functioning as a female body.
But all of us—male and female—are sinners who need reconciliation with God.
Our deepest uncleanness is not biological.
Jesus said evil proceeds from the human heart.
Paul wrote that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
That is the scandal beneath every other scandal.
We have sinned against a holy God.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something no amount of hiding could ever produce:
This is why the woman with the flow of blood is such a stunning picture of Christ's compassion.
Jesus was not contaminated into weakness by her touch.
His power moved toward her brokenness.
Her suffering did not frighten Him.
Her history did not repel Him.
Her body did not embarrass Him.
Her desperation did not annoy Him.
There is something beautiful happening here.
Shame says, “Don't let anyone see you.”
Shame reduces you to what happened to you.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being about that woman...
What have you been trying to hide from Jesus?
What have you spent years trying to repair without surrendering it to Christ?
What secret keeps whispering that if people really knew you, they would leave?
What sin have you renamed so you do not have to repent of it?
What wound have you allowed to become your identity?
The frightening part of grace is that God knows more about you than the people who rejected you ever knew...
and He still calls you to come.
Not to remain exactly as you are.
Grace is not permission to stay chained.
Grace brings us into the light.
Grace calls sin what God calls sin.
Grace does not merely cover your scandal.
grace begins rewriting what scandal tried to make the final chapter.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe somebody once made you ashamed of your body.
Jesus is not ashamed of the human body.
Think about the staggering humility of that sentence.
The eternal Son entered human biology.
And eventually, at Calvary, the One who stopped a woman's bleeding allowed His own blood to be shed.
Not because blood itself was shameful.

The blood at the cross was not menstrual blood, of course, and we should never collapse those categories. But Scripture's movement toward Christ gives us something infinitely greater than bodily symbolism:
the sinless Son of God willingly gave His life for sinners.
And the One who had once called a suffering woman “Daughter” endured the cross so that repentant sinners could be reconciled to the Father.
But declaring that Jesus Christ enters the places human beings hide and brings redemption there.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
Maybe it made you remember something.
Maybe you are a father realizing you need to speak differently to your daughter.
Maybe you are a husband realizing that jokes about your wife's body have hurt more than you understood.
Maybe you are a mother remembering the terrified girl you once were.
Maybe you are a young woman who needed somebody to tell you:
Your menstrual cycle does not make you morally filthy.
Your body is not an embarrassment to God.
And maybe you are carrying something much deeper than menstruation—something that actually does require confession, repentance, forgiveness, and healing.
Then don't hide behind this article either.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Jesus still meets people in places they thought were too embarrassing to bring into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish every private detail of your life on the internet. Wisdom still matters.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Somebody else may discover that they are not the only person fighting a battle nobody sees.
If you know a woman who grew up believing her body was somehow disgusting to God, send this to her.
If you know a father raising daughters, tag him.
If you know a believer who has confused ritual impurity in Leviticus with personal moral guilt, let this open a deeper conversation around Scripture.

Because one day a daughter, sister, wife, friend, teenager, new believer, or wounded Christian may ask you a question about this subject, and you may want to come back to these Scriptures instead of answering from embarrassment or inherited assumptions.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than fundraising:
Paul taught believers to give deliberately and willingly, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves cheerful giving.

So if you prayerfully choose to treat your monthly Gospel Warrior support as part of your personal generosity toward spreading biblical teaching, you are helping us continue creating and distributing Christ-centered resources. Whether and how that relates to your own practice of tithes and offerings is something you should determine faithfully before God and in keeping with your convictions and local church commitments.
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, supporting ministries that faithfully proclaim Christ is one meaningful way to steward what He has entrusted to you.
Somebody who cannot afford a library of Christian books can still encounter biblical teaching.
Somebody spiritually starving can find nourishment.
Somebody scrolling through Facebook at midnight while quietly losing hope can encounter the Gospel.
Somebody hiding can discover that Jesus is still calling people into the light.
That is why supporting, sharing, tagging, commenting, saving, and following matter.
Not because an algorithm is our god.
Because behind every number on a screen is a human being.
Someone who may be bleeding where nobody can see.
Come for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person standing metaphorically at the edge of the crowd.
Convinced they must somehow become presentable before approaching Jesus.
And perhaps the most important thing we can do is move aside...
The Bible never needed to erase women's bodies to protect God's holiness.
And Jesus never needed a suffering woman to disappear in order to preserve His dignity.
The story you thought could never be redeemed.
Because the thing you were terrified would make Jesus turn away may become the very place where you finally discover how closely grace has been standing.
You may have spent years hiding the stain, but Jesus has been looking for the person underneath it.
